The proposed legislation is somewhat of a departure from tradition in that it provides for Federal protection of all species and subspecies found by the Secretary to be endangered. After a State demonstrates an effective program to manage and protect an endangered species, the Secretary may suspend Federal jurisdiction for the species.
It should be pointed out that other than transfering authority for legal protection of endangered species to the Federal Government the proposed legislation in no way inhibits the States' traditional role as fish and wildlife managers. Habitat protection and improvement would be carried on by the States as well as Federal agencies. The legislation provides authority for the Secretary to enter into agreements with the States for administration and management of areas established for endangered species. The States would play a vital role in management of endangered animals within their boundaries.
Federal authority for resident fish and wildlife is specifically limited by the legislation to species and subspecies declared endangered. Effect of the impact will be dissatisfaction on the part of some State game and fish management agencies with the legislation. We believe much of this dissatisfaction can be allayed by prudent implementation of the provisions regarding State-Federal coordination.
